newsitem.title: JAPAN: Big Japanese realtor declared bankrupt.
newsitem.headline: Big Japanese realtor declared bankrupt.

text.p: A major Japanese realtor with debts of more than $6 billion, Sueno Kosan, has been declared bankrupt by a court, the semigovernmental Housing Loan Administration Corp (HLAC) said on Monday.

Private credit research agency Teikoku Databank Ltd said, meanwhile, that the failure of Sueno, whose debts total about 700 billion yen ($6.30 billion), was the second-largest insolvency case in Japan since World War Two.
Sueno, based in Osaka, western Japan, was a major borrower from failed "jusen" mortgage firms.
The declaration of insolvency came after the HLAC sought the involuntary bankruptcy of Sueno Kosan and its two units at the Osaka District Court last month.
An official at HLAC, set up to collect problem loans run up by the jusen firms earlier this year, told Reuters that Sueno's two units were also declared insolvent by the Osaka court.
Total debts of Sueno and its two units are about 970 billion yen ($8.73 billion), Teikoku Databank said.
In October, non-bank Nichiei Finance Co Ltd went under with total debts of about one trillion yen ($9.0 billion), the biggest bankruptcy case in Japan, it said.
Teikoku Databank said in a statement that Sueno Kosan, set up in February 1979, expanded its property business rapidly in the late 1980s "bubble" era of inflated stock and land prices.

But after the bursting of the bubble in the early 1990s and a protracted real estate market slump that ensued, its business deteriorated and it faced difficulty in raising funds, Teikoku Databank said.

The HLAC inherited assets totalling 6.5 trillion yen ($58.5 billion) from seven failed jusen under the government's scheme to wind up the firms after 6.4 trillion yen ($57.6 billion) worth of unrecoverable loans were written off with the help of banks and taxpayers' money.
The HLAC said it had claims totalling 347 billion yen ($3.12 billion) on Sueno Kosan and the two units.
Analysts said the insolvency of Sueno Kosan was not surprising following last month's action by the HLAC.

But they said individual non-bank financial institutions with outstanding loans to Sueno could suffer. A non-bank financial institutions makes loans but does not take deposits. It raises funds mainly by borrowing from banks. ($1=111 yen)
